content: Congenital ptosis is a condition characterized by the drooping of one or both eyelids present at birth. This condition is often caused by poor development of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, which is responsible for lifting the eyelid. If left untreated, congenital ptosis can lead to complications such as amblyopia (lazy eye), astigmatism, and ocular torticollis (abnormal head posture). In cases where visual development is at risk, surgical intervention during early childhood may be necessary. The severity of congenital ptosis varies, and patients exhibit different levels of levator muscle function. For individuals with moderate to good levator function, surgical options such as external levator advancement or mullerectomy/Fasanella–Servat procedures may be attempted. However, for patients with poor levator function, these procedures are less effective. In such cases, frontalis sling surgery is often performed. This procedure involves connecting the tarsal plate of the eyelid to the frontalis muscle in the forehead, allowing the eyelid to be elevated through the movement of the brow and forehead. Despite its widespread use, the optimal material for frontalis sling surgery remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of various materials used in frontalis sling surgery for congenital ptosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, was conducted. The search included studies published up to June 20, 2018, without restrictions on language or publication date. Randomized controlled trials comparing different materials for frontalis sling surgery were included in the analysis. Three randomized trials were identified, involving a total of 160 participants. These studies compared four different materials: polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex), Ethibond suture, Mersilene mesh, and autogenous fascia lata. However, all three studies were judged to have an unclear risk of bias due to incomplete reporting of methods and other methodological limitations. Because each study compared different materials, the data could not be combined into a meta-analysis, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the optimal material for this procedure. The primary outcome assessed in these studies was functional success, defined as an increase in the eyelid opening, measured either by grade or in millimeters. In the study by Bajaj (2004), 93% of patients in the Gore-Tex group and 83% in the Ethibond group achieved good or satisfactory outcomes. Elsamkary (2016) reported that 78.1% of patients in the autogenous fascia lata group and 61.8% in the Gore-Tex group had very good or good outcomes. Salour (2008) did not use a grading system but reported an increase in lid fissure width of 4.0 mm ± 1.46 mm in the Mersilene group and 3.13 mm ± 1.72 mm in the fascia lata group. Adverse events were also reported. In Bajaj (2004), which included 15 patients per group, there were no recurrences, infections, or removals in the Gore-Tex group, while the Ethibond group had one recurrence, one removal, and one infection. Elsamkary (2016), which included 55 patients per group, reported three recurrences in the fascia lata group and six in the Gore-Tex group, with no removals in either group and one infection in the fascia lata group compared to two in the Gore-Tex group. Salour (2008), which included 10 patients per group, reported no recurrences, removals, or infections in either the Mersilene or fascia lata groups. In conclusion, the three trials reviewed evaluated four different materials for frontalis sling surgery. However, due to the limited data and methodological shortcomings of the studies, it is not possible to determine the optimal material for this procedure. Future randomized trials should be designed with rigorous methodology to identify the most effective and safe material for frontalis sling surgery in patients with congenital ptosis.
